Its intelligence therefore seems puzzling.
exercicios.exp: O contexto: mamíferos e aves são inteligentes por causa da vida social, mas o polvo é solitário. 'Puzzling' liga com 'The puzzle' e prepara a teoria.

exercicios.resp: If so intelligence in this lineage may have evolved more than once
exercicios.exp: If so retoma a ideia anterior. Sem a pergunta, o sentido: se isso é verdade.

exercicios.q: The soft-body theory does not explain why squid, ___ share the octopus's soft body, behave less cleverly.
exercicios.exp: Oração relativa não restritiva: squid, which share... O pronome which retoma squid.

exercicios.q: Do you think animals like octopuses should have the same legal protection as other animals? Give reasons.
exercicios.frase: Do you think animals like octopuses should have the same legal protection as other animals? Give reasons.
exercicios.modelo: Yes, I think so, because if they can feel pain and form relationships, it would be wrong to treat them badly.
exercicios.exp: Dê opinião e razão. Use if they can... it would be wrong to... Pode usar a ideia de consciência do texto.

exercicios.q: Which sentence best fits gap (D)?
op: The finding is of interest to chefs only.
The idea is as unsettling as it is thrilling.
Octopuses are not alien at all.
No one has studied the subject.
exercicios.exp: O trecho anterior diz 'intelligent alien'; o seguinte fala de 'awkward questions'. A frase deve conter ideia de impacto intelectual: unsettling e thrilling.

exercicios.q: Not only ___ the octopus a solitary animal, but it also lives for barely two years.
exercicios.exp: Not only no início exige inversão: is the octopus. Sem inversão seria: The octopus is not only solitary but...

aulas.objetivo: Comparar opiniões sutis de vários autores e identificar quem concorda ou discorda em pontos específicos.
aulas.foco: Multiple matching: stance, implication and paraphrase
explicacao: Em multiple matching, a resposta usa paráfrase: 'forces me to decide what I mean' = 'slows down the writer and improves thinking'.
Cuidado com palavras iguais em textos diferentes: dois autores podem usar 'pen' com ideias opostas.
Identifique a postura de cada autor: cético, nostálgico, pragmático, solidário. Depois procure o ponto em comum e a diferença.
Uma frase como 'I am not a sentimental man' mostra que o autor aceita um argumento, mas por outra razão.

material.texto:
Handwriting is, for the first time in history, optional. A generation of children now learns to type before it learns to join letters, and the signature on a document may be the last thing many of us write by hand all week. Four writers consider what, if anything, is lost.

A. Teodoro Brandt. I am not a sentimental man, and I resist the idea that the pen has a mystical bond with the mind. But I notice that when I draft a letter by hand, I write less and think more. The slowness is an obstacle that forces me to decide what I mean before I commit it to paper. On a keyboard I produce paragraphs I would never have written had I been obliged to form each word. The difference is not nostalgia; it is discipline, and discipline is in short supply.

B. Leona Marsh. Teachers tell me that handwriting improves spelling and memory, and I do not doubt it. What troubles me is how readily such claims are used to dismiss the technology that is, after all, the way most of us now write. Typing is not the enemy of thought. It has made writing available to people who found the pen a torment, whether through disability or sheer clumsiness. If something has been lost, something has also been gained, and the account should be kept honestly on both sides.

C. Ahmad Farouk. I received a letter last year from my mother, who is eighty-six. Her hand has become unsteady, and the lines slope down the page like a tired walker. I read it four times. No message sent on a screen has ever carried so much information about its sender, and the information was not in the words. Handwriting is a form of presence. We may be right to give it up for most purposes, but we should not pretend that it was merely a clumsier way of doing what typing does better.

D. Priya Venkataraman. I teach adults who have never learned to write, and for them the pen is not a nostalgia but a door. The first time one of my students signs her own name, the room goes quiet. I would not want to lecture anyone about the virtues of old methods, but I wish the debate would remember that in much of the world, literacy still begins with a pencil. Before we mourn a skill, we might ask who has yet to acquire it.

The question each of them raises is not really about technology at all. It is about what we are prepared to do slowly, and why.

exercicios.q: Which writer says that handwriting makes writers think more carefully?
op: A
B
C
D
exercicios.exp: Brandt: 'when I draft a letter by hand, I write less and think more'. A lentidão obriga a decidir o que se quer dizer.

exercicios.q: Writer B suggests that typing has made writing accessible to people who found the pen a ___ .
exercicios.exp: Marsh diz que a escrita ficou acessível a quem achava a caneta 'a torment'.

exercicios.q: Leia em voz alta esta frase.
exercicios.frase: We may be right to give it up for most purposes, but we should not pretend it was merely a clumsier way of doing what typing does better.
exercicios.exp: Frase longa: respire em 'purposes'. Clumsier: CLÂM-zi-er. Mantenha o contraste com 'but'.

exercicios.q: Which two writers both express concern that the debate may be one-sided?
op: A and C
A and B
C and D
B and D
exercicios.exp: Marsh quer manter a conta 'honestly on both sides' e Venkataraman pede que o debate lembre quem ainda não aprendeu. Ambos pedem um debate mais completo.

exercicios.resp: Before we mourn a skill we might ask who has yet to acquire it
exercicios.exp: Venkataraman reorienta a discussão: antes de lamentar a perda de uma habilidade, perguntar quem ainda não a tem.

exercicios.q: Writer C values handwriting because it reveals information about the sender that is not in the ___ .
exercicios.exp: Farouk: 'the information was not in the words'. Isso é presença.

exercicios.q: Which of the four writers do you agree with most, and why?
exercicios.frase: Which of the four writers do you agree with most, and why?
exercicios.modelo: I agree most with writer B, because technology has helped many people, even though handwriting still has some value.
exercicios.exp: Escolha um autor e justifique com paráfrase. Use I agree most with... because..., although.

exercicios.q: Which writer implies that the loss of handwriting is being discussed from a privileged perspective?
op: Brandt
Farouk
Marsh
Venkataraman
exercicios.exp: Venkataraman lembra que em grande parte do mundo a alfabetização ainda começa com o lápis, ou seja, quem lamenta já tem a habilidade.

exercicios.q: The final sentence says the question is really about what we are prepared to do ___ .
exercicios.exp: Fecho do texto: 'what we are prepared to do slowly, and why'. Une as quatro opiniões.

aulas.titulo: Mock exam: Reading and Use of English
aulas.objetivo: Fazer um simulado com partes do C2 Proficiency: cloze, open cloze, word formation, key word transformation, texto longo, frase faltando e matching.
aulas.foco: Exam practice: Parts 1 to 7 of Reading and Use of English
explicacao: Part 1: escolha a palavra que combina (collocation, nuance) e não só a que tem o significado certo.
Parts 2 e 3: decida a classe gramatical da lacuna antes de preencher; em Part 3, cuide dos prefixos negativos e do plural.
Part 4: a segunda frase deve ter o mesmo sentido, com a palavra-chave inalterada e 3 a 5 palavras.
Parts 5 a 7: leia o texto todo, procure a paráfrase (não palavras iguais) e confira conectivos, pronomes e o tom do autor.

material.texto:
[1] When the photograph was invented, it was greeted by some as the end of forgetting. Here, at last, was a way to fix a moment so that it could be recalled in every detail, and the Victorians, who adored any machine that promised permanence, took to the camera with a fervour that bordered on devotion. A century and a half later, we take roughly two trillion pictures a year, and the question that was once raised in wonder is now raised in doubt: do all these images help us to remember, or do they quietly take the place of remembering?

[2] The evidence, such as it is, points in an uncomfortable direction. In a widely cited experiment, visitors to a museum were asked to photograph some exhibits and merely look at others. When tested the following day, they remembered fewer of the objects they had photographed, and fewer details of those they could recall. Psychologists call this the photo-taking impairment effect. The explanation is not complicated: having handed the task of remembering to the device, the mind feels entitled to put its feet up. What is odd is that the effect largely disappeared when the participants were allowed to zoom in on a particular detail, as though a small act of choosing were enough to restore attention.

[3] It would be a mistake, however, to conclude that the camera is the villain of the story. Photographs are, among other things, an extraordinary prompt. A faded picture of a kitchen can unlock a whole afternoon of smells and voices that would otherwise have stayed buried, and many of us would be poorer without the images that tie us to people no longer alive. The danger lies not in the picture but in the habit of treating the picture as the memory itself. A snapshot records what a place looked like; it says nothing of what it was like to be there, and the longer we look at the one, the more the other tends to fade.

[4] There is also the question of what we choose to preserve. The family album of an earlier age was a modest affair, a few dozen carefully chosen images of weddings and holidays, and its very scarcity gave each picture weight. The modern phone contains ten thousand pictures, most of which will never be looked at again. The result is a curious kind of abundance that resembles poverty: so much is kept that nothing is cherished. One suspects that the great-grandchildren who inherit these archives will be less moved by the quantity than their ancestors were by the little leather book on the mantelpiece.

[5] None of this requires us to put away our cameras. What it suggests is a measure of restraint, and perhaps a small ritual: to take one photograph, rather than twenty, and then to put the phone away and look. If the research is right, the looking is what makes the keeping possible. A picture can only remind us of a moment we have in some sense lived, and the only reliable way of living a moment is to be present while it lasts. It is an old piece of advice, and, like most old advice, it is easier to admire than to follow.

exercicios.q: PART 1 (multiple-choice cloze). 'The Victorians took to the camera with a ___ that bordered on devotion.' Choose the word that best fits.

fuss
fervour
fixation
exercicios.exp: Fervour (ardor) combina com 'bordered on devotion'. Frenzy é descontrolado e negativo; fuss e fixation não combinam.

To criticise psychologists for ignoring the camera.

To present evidence that taking pictures can weaken recall.

op: Only poor families take many pictures.
Old albums were richer than modern ones in every sense.
Large collections of pictures are too expensive to store.
When too much is kept, nothing is valued.

Few people keep photographs these days.
Cameras should therefore be banned from museums.
